nodes.name: Guessing game
nodes.statement: The guessing game was introduced by Riis in 2007 \cite{Riis2007information}. It is a cooperative $n$-player information game played on a graph with $n$ vertices with $s$ colours.
differentia: played on a graph with $n$ vertices with $s$ colours

nodes.name: Deterministic protocols are optimal for the guessing game
nodes.statement: It is known that the greatest probability of winning the guessing game can be achieved by a deterministic protocol \cite{Cameron2014guessing}.
conclusions: the greatest probability of winning the guessing game can be achieved by a deterministic protocol

nodes.name: Graph notation $G=(V,E)$
nodes.statement: Let $G = (V,E)$ be a graph where $V = \{ v_1,v_2, \ldots ,v_n \}$ is the set of vertices and $E \subseteq \binom{V}{2}$ is the edge set.

nodes.name: Protocol, colouring, fixed set
nodes.statement: For any positive integer $s$, we let $\mathbb{Z}_s$, the group of all residues modulo $s$, denote the \emph{colour set}. A \emph{colouring} of $G$ with $s$ colours is an $n$-tuple $c = (c_1,c_2, \ldots ,c_n)$ such that $c_i \in \mathbb{Z}_s$. The set of all colourings of $G$ with $s$ colours is denoted $\mathbb{Z}_s^n$. A \emph{protocol} on $G$ with $s$ colours is any $n$-tuple $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2,f_3, \ldots ,f_n)$ where for each $i$, the [deterministic] function $f_i : \mathbb{Z}_s^n \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_s$ is such that $f_i(c)$ is dependent only on $c_j$ for all $j$ such that $v_iv_j \in E$, {\it i.e.} for any $i$ and any two colourings $c = (c_1,c_2, \ldots ,c_n)$ and $c^\prime = (c_1^\prime,c_2^\prime,\ldots ,c_n^\prime)$, if $c_j^\prime = c_j$ for all $j$ such that $v_iv_j \in E$ then $f_i(c) = f_i(c^\prime)$. The \emph{fixed set} of $\mathcal{P}$, $\mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$, is the set of all invariant colourings: $$ \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}) = \big\{ c \in \mathbb{Z}_s^n \: | \: c_i=f_i(c) \; \forall i \big\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Colourings are $n$-tuples over $\mathbb{Z}_s$; a protocol assigns each vertex a guess depending only on its neighbours' colours; Fix(P) is the set of correctly guessed colourings.
nodes.label: defn:prot

nodes.name: Fixed number, non-trivial and optimal protocol
nodes.statement: The \emph{fixed number} of $\mathcal{P}$ is the size of its fixed set; $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) = |\mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})|$. A protocol $\mathcal{P}$ is called \emph{non-trivial} if $\mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}) \not= \emptyset$. A protocol is called \emph{optimal} if it has maximal fixed number.
nodes.label: defn:gn

nodes.name: Guessing number
nodes.statement: The \emph{guessing number} of $G$ with $s$ colours is defined as $$ \mbox{gn}(G,s) = \log_s \max_{\mathcal{P}} \left[ \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \right]. $$
nodes.statement_short: gn(G,s) is the base-$s$ log of the maximum fixed number over all protocols.
nodes.label: defn:fixed

nodes.name: Winning probability of an optimal protocol
nodes.statement: We assign the $n$-tuple of colours $c \in \mathbb{Z}_s^n$ uniformly at random to the set of players, who are each identified with a vertex of $G$. The guesses of the players are given by $\mathcal{P}(c)$, so the players win if and only if $c = \mathcal{P}(c)$. Hence, the probability that an optimal protocol $\mathcal{P}$ wins is $$ \mathbb{P}\big(c = \mathcal{P}(c)\big) = \frac{\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})}{|\mathbb{Z}_s^n|} = s^{\mbox{gn}(G,s)-n}. $$
nodes.statement_short: With uniformly random colours, an optimal protocol wins with probability $s^{gn(G,s)-n}$.

nodes.name: Guessing number of perfect graphs
nodes.statement: Christofides and Markstr\"{o}m \cite{Christofides2011guessing} showed that, for a perfect graph $G$ and any $s$, $\mbox{gn}(G,s) = n-\alpha$ where $\alpha$ is the size of the largest independent set in $G$.
assumptions: for a perfect graph $G$ and any $s$
conclusions: $\mbox{gn}(G,s) = n-\alpha$ where $\alpha$ is the size of the largest independent set in $G$

nodes.name: Complete graph $K_n$
nodes.statement: For example, the complete graph $K_n$ is a perfect graph with $\alpha = 1$, so an optimal protocol on $K_n$, wins with probability $1/s$.

nodes.name: Guessing numbers of $C_3$ and even cycles
nodes.statement: The $3$-cycle and the even-cycle $C_{2k}$ (for any positive integer $k$) are both perfect graphs with $\alpha(C_3)=1$ and $\alpha(C_{2k})=k$ so \begin{equation} \mbox{gn}(C_3,s) = 2 \quad \mbox{and} \quad \mbox{gn}(C_{2k},s)=k \quad \forall \: k. \end{equation}
assumptions: The $3$-cycle and the even-cycle $C_{2k}$ (for any positive integer $k$) are both perfect graphs

nodes.name: Guessing numbers of $C_3$ and $C_{2k}$
nodes.statement: \mbox{gn}(C_3,s) = 2 \quad \mbox{and} \quad \mbox{gn}(C_{2k},s)=k \quad \forall \: k.
nodes.label: eq:perfect_graphs

nodes.name: Guessing numbers of odd cycles with two colours
nodes.statement: In \cite{Christofides2011guessing}, it is shown that $$\mbox{gn}(C_5,2) =5,$$ and the analysis in \cite{bar2011index} shows that $$\mbox{gn}(C_n,2) = \frac{n-1}{2},\;\; \mbox{for odd }n\geq 7. $$
assumptions: for odd }n\geq 7

nodes.name: Fractional-clique strategy is optimal for perfect-square colour numbers
nodes.statement: The fractional clique strategy is only defined when the number of colours $s$ is a perfect power, and it is shown to be optimal on the odd cycle whenever $s$ is a perfect square, {\it i.e.} \begin{equation} \mbox{gn}(C_n,m^2) = \frac{n}{2} \qquad \forall \: n,m. \end{equation}
assumptions: $s$ is a perfect square
conclusions: it is shown to be optimal on the odd cycle
nodes.statement_short: The fractional-clique strategy is optimal on odd cycles when $s=m^2$, so gn$(C_n,m^2)=n/2$.

nodes.name: Guessing number of cycles with a square number of colours
nodes.statement: \mbox{gn}(C_n,m^2) = \frac{n}{2} \qquad \forall \: n,m.
nodes.label: eq:s_square

nodes.name: Relation of $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ to the clique strategies
nodes.statement: The protocol $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ is equivalent to the clique-strategy when $s$ is prime, and to the fractional-clique-strategy when $s$ is a perfect square.

nodes.name: Forgetting colours (monotonicity in $s$)
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a graph, let $s$ and $s^\prime$ be positive integers with $s^\prime \leq s$, and let $\mathcal{P}$ be any protocol on $G$ with $s$ colours. There exists a protocol $\mathcal{P}^\prime$ on $G$ with $s^\prime$ colours such that $$ \big\{ c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}) \: \big| \: 0 \leq c_i < s^\prime \: \forall i \big\} \subseteq \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime). $$
assumptions: $G$ be a graph
$s$ and $s^\prime$ be positive integers with $s^\prime \leq s$
$\mathcal{P}$ be any protocol on $G$ with $s$ colours
conclusions: There exists a protocol $\mathcal{P}^\prime$ on $G$ with $s^\prime$ colours such that $$ \big\{ c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}) \: \big| \: 0 \leq c_i < s^\prime \: \forall i \big\} \subseteq \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime). $$
nodes.statement_short: Any $s$-colour protocol yields an $s'$-colour protocol ($s'\le s$) fixing all its fixed colourings that use only colours below $s'$.
nodes.label: prop:monotone

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots f_n)$ then define $\mathcal{P}^\prime = (f_1^\prime,f_2^\prime, \ldots ,f_n^\prime )$ in the following way. \begin{itemize} \item If $0 \leq c_j<s^\prime$ for all $j$ such that $v_iv_j \in E$, and $0 \leq f_i(c)<s^\prime$ then $f_i^\prime(c) = f_i(c)$. \item If $s^\prime \leq c_j < s$ for any $j$ such that $v_iv_j \in E$, or $s^\prime \leq f_i(c) < s$ then $f_i^\prime(c) = 0$. \end{itemize} For any colouring $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$, if $0 \leq c_i < s^\prime$ for all $i$, then $\mathcal{P}^\prime(c) = \mathcal{P}(c) = c$ so $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime)$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\mathcal{P}'$ by keeping $f_i$ when all inputs and output are below $s'$ and guessing 0 otherwise.

nodes.name: Entropy, mutual information
nodes.statement: Let $A_1, \ldots, A_k$ be random variables which take values in a finite set $\mathcal{A}$. The \emph{entropy} of $A_1,\ldots, A_k$ is denoted $H(A_1,\ldots, A_k)$ and is given by: $$ H(A_1,\ldots,A_k) = -\sum_{a_1,\ldots,a_k \in \mathcal{A}^k} \mathbb{P}(A_1=a_1,\ldots,A_k=a_k) \log_s \mathbb{P}(A_1=a_1,\ldots,A_k=a_k). $$ The \emph{mutual information} of $A_1$ and $A_2$ is denoted $I(A_1;A_2)$ and is given by: $$ I(A_1;A_2) = H(A_1) + H(A_2) - H(A_1,A_2). $$ Let $B$ be another random variable taking values in $\mathcal{A}$. The conditional mutual information of $I(A_1;A_2|B)$ is given by \begin{equation} I(A_1;A_2|B) = H(A_1,B) + H(A_2,B) - H(A_1,A_2,B) - H(B). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Base-$s$ Shannon entropy, mutual information $I(A_1;A_2)$ and conditional mutual information $I(A_1;A_2|B)$.
nodes.label: defn:entropy

nodes.name: Basic entropy inequalities (Shannon's inequality)
nodes.statement: Let $A_1$, $A_2$ be random variables which take values in a finite sets $\mathcal{A}$. \begin{enumerate} \item $H(A_1) \leq \log |\mathcal{A}|$ with equality if and only if $A_1$ is uniformly distributed. \item $I(A_1;A_2) \geq 0$ with equality if and only if $A_1$ and $A_2$ are independent. \item $I(A_1;A_2|B) \geq 0$ with equality if and only if $A_1$ and $A_2$ are independent conditional on $B$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $A_1$, $A_2$ be random variables which take values in a finite sets $\mathcal{A}$
conclusions: $H(A_1) \leq \log |\mathcal{A}|$ with equality if and only if $A_1$ is uniformly distributed
$I(A_1;A_2) \geq 0$ with equality if and only if $A_1$ and $A_2$ are independent
$I(A_1;A_2|B) \geq 0$ with equality if and only if $A_1$ and $A_2$ are independent conditional on $B$
nodes.statement_short: Entropy is at most log of alphabet size; (conditional) mutual information is nonnegative, zero iff (conditional) independence.
nodes.label: prop:known_entropy_results

nodes.name: Uniform random variable notation $\in_u$
nodes.statement: For a non-empty set $S$, we use the notation $A \in_u S$ to mean $A$ is a random variable distributed uniformly over all elements in $S$.

nodes.name: Notation for $C_n$
nodes.statement: The cycle graph, $C_n$, has $n$ vertices $V = \{ v_1,v_2, \ldots ,v_n \}$. The edge set of $C_n$ is $$ E = \{ v_iv_{i+1} \: | \: i = 1,2,3, \ldots ,n \} $$ (indices are always taken modulo $n$). In a slight abuse of notation, for any protocol $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2,f_3, \ldots ,f_n)$ on $C_n$ with $s$ colours, we say $f_i : \mathbb{Z}_s^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_s$ where $$ f_i(c) = f_i(c_{i-1},c_{i+1}). $$ Recall that a protocol $\mathcal{P}$ is non-trivial if $\mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}) \neq \emptyset$. For a given non-trivial protocol $\mathcal{P}$ on $C_n$, define $X = (X_1,X_2, \ldots ,X_n)$ to be a colouring chosen uniformly at random from $\mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$. \emph{i.e.} $$ X \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}). $$ Note that the random colouring $X = (X_1,X_2, \ldots ,X_n)$ is only defined for non-trivial protocols $\mathcal{P}$. To simplify notation we will sometimes denote the entropy of a tuple of $X_i$s by $$ h(i_1,i_2,i_3, \ldots ) = H(X_{i_1},X_{i_2},X_{i_3}, \ldots ). $$ Since $X_i$ is determined by $(X_{i-1},X_{i+1})$ we must have $H(X_{i-1},X_i,X_{i+1}) = H(X_{i-1},X_{i+1})$ so $h(i-1,i,i+1)=h(i-1,i+1)$. In general we can freely remove the argument $i$ from $h( \ldots , i-1 , i , i+1 , \ldots )$ as long as we don't remove the arguments $i-1$ and $i+1$. \begin{equation} h( \ldots , i-1 , i , i+1 , \ldots ) = h( \ldots , i-1 , i+1 , \ldots ) \end{equation} To simplify notation even further, for integers $j<k$, let $H_j^k$ denote the quantity $$ H_j^k = h(j,j+1,j+2, \ldots ,k-1) + h(j+1,j+2,j+3, \ldots ,k). $$
nodes.statement_short: Cycle $C_n$, protocols as $f_i(c_{i-1},c_{i+1})$, $X$ uniform on Fix(P), shorthand $h(\cdot)$ for joint entropies and $H_j^k$ for sums of two window entropies.
nodes.label: defn:C_n

nodes.name: Removing a determined index from $h$
nodes.statement: h( \ldots , i-1 , i , i+1 , \ldots ) = h( \ldots , i-1 , i+1 , \ldots )
nodes.label: eq:awesome

nodes.name: Subadditivity of $H_i^k$
nodes.statement: For any three integers $i,j,k$ such that $1 \leq i < j$ and $j+1 < k \leq n$. $$ H_i^k \leq H_i^j + H_{j+1}^k. $$
assumptions: three integers $i,j,k$ such that $1 \leq i < j$ and $j+1 < k \leq n$
nodes.label: prop:H=sum(H)

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: We add up the following inequalities: \begin{align*} h(i,i+1, \ldots , k-1) & = h(i, \ldots ,j-1,j+1, \ldots , k-1) \\ & \leq h(i, \ldots ,j-1) + h(j+1 \ldots , k-1), \\ \mbox{and} \quad h(i+1,i+2, \ldots , k) & = h(i+1, \ldots ,j,j+2, \ldots , k) \\ & \leq h(i+1, \ldots ,j) + h(j+2, \ldots , k). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Remove index $j$ (resp. $j+1$) using (2.2), then apply subadditivity of entropy and add.

nodes.name: Entropy of a uniform fixed colouring
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{P}$ is a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$, then, for all $i$, $$\log_s \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) = H(X), \;\; h(i) \leq 1.$$
assumptions: $\mathcal{P}$ is a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$
nodes.label: lem:H(X),h(i)

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.7
nodes.statement: The entropy of any random variable over a finite domain is maximised when the variable is uniformly distributed. Therefore, $h(i) = H(X_i) \leq H(U)$ where $U$ is a random variable uniformly distributed over $\mathbb{Z}_s$. Hence, $$ h(i) \leq H(U) = - \sum \frac{1}{s} \log_s \frac{1}{s} = 1. $$ The variable $X$ is uniformly distributed over $\mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$. Therefore, $$ H(X) = - \sum \frac{1}{\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})} \log_s \frac{1}{\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})} = \log_s \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}). $$
nodes.statement_short: Entropy is maximised by the uniform distribution; compute the entropy of uniform variables directly.

nodes.name: $H_j^k$ bounded by sum of single entropies
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{P}$ is a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$, then $$ H_j^k \leq \sum_{i=j}^{k} H(X_i) ,$$ for any $j \leq 1$ and $j+3 \leq k \leq n$.
assumptions: $\mathcal{P}$ is a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$
for any $j \leq 1$ and $j+3 \leq k \leq n$
nodes.label: lem:H_j^k<sum(h(i))

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.8
nodes.statement: We prove this by induction on $(k-j)$. Recall that $h(i_1,i_2,i_3, \ldots ) = H(X_{i_1},X_{i_2},X_{i_3}, \ldots )$. \begin{itemize} \item {\bf Base case: }$k=j+3$. Since $X_{j+1} = f_{j+1}(X_j,X_{j+2})$ and $X_{j+2} = f_{j+2}(X_{j+1},X_{j+3})$ we have \begin{align*} h(j,j+1,j+2) = h(j,j+2) & \leq h(j)+h(j+2) \\ \mbox{and} \qquad h(j+1,j+2,j+3) = h(j+1,j+3) & \leq h(j+1)+h(j+3) , \end{align*} respectively. Adding these together yields: $$ H_j^{j+3} = h(j,j+1,j+2) + h(j+1,j+2,j+3) \leq h(j)+h(j+1)+h(j+2)+h(j+3). $$ \item {\bf Inductive step:} $k \geq j+4$. Since $X_{k-1} = f_{k-1}(X_{k-2},X_k)$ we have \begin{align*} h(j+1,j+2, \ldots ,k) & = h(j+1,j+2, \ldots ,k-2,k) \\ & \leq h(j+1,j+2, \ldots ,k-2)+h(k). \end{align*} By Proposition~\ref{prop:known_entropy_results}, $ I(X_j ; X_{k-1} | X_{j+1},X_{j+2}, \ldots ,X_{k-2})\geq 0$. Adding these together yields $$ H_j^k \leq H_j^{k-1} + h(k). $$ This completes the proof. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k-j$: base case $k=j+3$ via determinism of $X_{j+1},X_{j+2}$; inductive step drops $X_{k-1}$ and uses nonnegative conditional mutual information.

nodes.name: Decomposition of $2\log_s \mathrm{fix}(\mathcal{P})$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and let $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$. Suppose $1 = d(1),d(2),d(3), \ldots ,d(k) = n$ is a sequence of positive integers with $k \geq 2$. If $d(i+1) \geq d(i)+2$ for all $i$, then $$ 2\log_s\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) = H_{d(1)}^{d(2)} + H_{d(2)+1}^{d(3)} + \cdots + H_{d(k-1)+1}^{d(k)}. $$
assumptions: $\mathcal{P}$ be a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and let $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$
$1 = d(1),d(2),d(3), \ldots ,d(k) = n$ is a sequence of positive integers with $k \geq 2$
$d(i+1) \geq d(i)+2$ for all $i$
nodes.label: lem:H(X)=sum(H)

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.9
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $k$. \begin{itemize} \item {\bf Base case:} $k=2$. Since $X_1 = f_1(X_n,X_2)$ and $X_n = f_n(X_{n-1},X_1)$, we have $$ H(X) = h(2,3,4, \ldots ,n) \qquad \mbox{and} \qquad H(X) = h(1,2,3, \ldots ,n-1) ,$$ respectively. Adding these together gives $H_1^n = 2H(X) = 2\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$. \item {\bf Inductive step.} By Proposition \ref{prop:H=sum(H)}, for any $d(k-1)+2 \leq d(k) \leq n-2$, we have $$ H_{d(k-1)+1}^{n} = H_{d(k-1)+1}^{d(k)} + H_{d(k)+1}^{n}. $$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$: base case from $X_1$, $X_n$ being determined by neighbours; inductive step splits via Proposition 2.6.

nodes.name: Factorization bijection
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that for any factorization $ab=s$, there exists a bijection between $\mathbb{Z}_s$ and $\mathbb{Z}_a \times \mathbb{Z}_b$. Let $\phi(z) \times \psi(z)$ be such a bijection. For ease of notation, $a$ and $b$ are assumed to be given in context. Let $\pi$ be the inverse of this bijection, so that $\pi(\phi(z),\psi(z))=z$ for all $z \in \mathbb{Z}_s$.
nodes.statement_short: For $ab=s$, fix a bijection $\phi\times\psi:\mathbb{Z}_s\to\mathbb{Z}_a\times\mathbb{Z}_b$ with inverse $\pi$.
nodes.label: defn:phi_and_psi

nodes.name: Fractional-clique-partition protocol
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 3$ be an odd integer, let $s$ be a positive integer, let $a$ be the greatest factor of $s$ less than or equal to $\sqrt{s}$ and let $b = s/a$. For any colouring $c = (c_1,c_2, \ldots ,c_n) \in \mathbb{Z}_s^n$, let $\phi(c_i)$ and $\psi(c_i)$ be referred to as the first and second coordinates respectively of vertex $v_i$. The \emph{fractional-clique-partition protocol} is the protocol $\mathcal{P}_{fcp} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ on $C_n$ defined by: \begin{align*} f_i(c_{i-1},c_{i+1}) & = \pi \big( \phi(c_{i-1}) , \psi(c_{i+1}) \big) & \mbox{for } i=2,4,6, \ldots ,n-1 \\ f_i(c_{i-1},c_{i+1}) & = \pi \big( \phi(c_{i+1}) , \psi(c_{i-1}) \big) & \mbox{for } i=3,5,7, \ldots ,n-2 \\ f_1(c_n,c_2) & = \pi \big( \phi(c_2) , \phi(c_n) \big) & \mbox{and} \\ f_n(c_{n-1},c_1) & = \pi \big( \psi(c_1) (\mbox{mod } a), \psi(c_{n-1}) \big). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: On odd $C_n$, split each colour into coordinates in $\mathbb{Z}_a\times\mathbb{Z}_b$; neighbouring vertices alternately copy first and second coordinates, with $v_1,v_n$ copying as much as possible.
nodes.label: defn:P_fcp

nodes.name: Informal description of $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$
nodes.statement: Informally, vertices $v_{2k-1}$ and $v_{2k}$ are copying each others first coordinate and vertices $v_{2k}$ and $v_{2k+1}$ are copying each others second coordinate (for $k = 1,2,3, \ldots , (n-1)/2$). Additionally, the second coordinate of vertex $v_1$ and the first coordinate of vertex $v_n$ copy each other as much as possible - whenever the second coordinate of vertex $v_1$ is less than $a$.
nodes.statement_short: In $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ consecutive vertex pairs copy alternately first and second coordinates; $v_1$ and $v_n$ copy whenever possible.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ on $C_7$
nodes.statement: The protocol $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ on $C_7$ with $s=ab$ colours, where $a<b$. Each vertex $v_i$ is subdivided into two nodes representing the first and second components ($\phi(c_i)$ and $\psi(c_i)$, respectively). The red edges (\tikz[baseline=-0.5ex]{ \draw[densely dotted,red!70,line width=3pt] (0,0) -- (.5,0); }) represent pairs of first-components that are copying each other. The blue edges (\tikz[baseline=-0.5ex]{ \draw[loosely dotted,blue!70,line width=3pt] (0,0) -- (.5,0); }) represent pairs of second-components that are copying each other. The black edge (\tikz[baseline=-0.5ex]{ \draw[black!100,line width=3pt] (0,0) -- (.5,0); }) joins a first-component ($\phi(c_n)$) and a second-component ($\psi(c_1)$) which are copying each other as much as possible. For a colouring $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp})$ on $C_7$, there are $a$ different choices for each red edge, $b$ different choices for each blue edge and $a$ different choices for the black edge. Therefore, $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp}) = a^4b^3=as^3$ for $n=7$.
nodes.statement_short: Figure caption: $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ on $C_7$ has $a^4b^3=as^3$ fixed colourings.

nodes.name: Fixed number of $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$
nodes.statement: For a given integer $s \geq 2$ and odd integer $n \geq 3$, if $a$ is the greatest factor of $s$ less than or equal to $\sqrt{s}$, then we have $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp}) = as^{(n-1)/2}$.
assumptions: a given integer $s \geq 2$ and odd integer $n \geq 3$
$a$ is the greatest factor of $s$ less than or equal to $\sqrt{s}$
nodes.label: prop:fix_Ffcp

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: Let $n = 2k+1$. We count the number of colourings of $C_n$ for which the protocol $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ guesses correctly. For any colouring $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp})$, there are $k$ pairs of vertices copying each other's first coordinates and there are $a$ different choices for $\phi$ for each pair. Similarly, for each of the $k$ pairs of vertices copying each other's second coordinates, there are $b$ different choices for $\psi$. This yields $a^kb^k$ possibilities. Additionally, the first coordinate of vertex $v_n$ must equal the second coordinate of vertex $v_1$, for which there are $a$ possible colours. Multiplying these together yields $$ \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp}) = a^{k+1}b^k = as^{(n-1)/2}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Count fixed colourings: $a$ choices per first-coordinate pair, $b$ per second-coordinate pair, and $a$ for the $v_1$--$v_n$ link.

nodes.name: Upper bound $\mathrm{gn}(C_n,s)\le n/2$
nodes.statement: \cite{Christofides2011guessing} For any integer $n \geq 4$, we have $\displaystyle{\mbox{gn}(C_n,s) \leq \tfrac{n}{2}}$, with equality only if for any optimal protocol, $\mathcal{P}$ the following is satisfied. If $X \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$ then $H(X_i)=1$ for all $i$.
assumptions: any integer $n \geq 4$
conclusions: with equality only if for any optimal protocol, $\mathcal{P}$ the following is satisfied. If $X \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$ then $H(X_i)=1$ for all $i$.
nodes.label: thm:n/2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.4
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be an optimal protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:H(X),h(i)},~\ref{lem:H_j^k<sum(h(i))} and ~\ref{lem:H(X)=sum(H)}, we have $$ \mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = \log_s\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) = H(X) = \tfrac{1}{2} H_1^n \leq \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n h(i) \leq \frac{n}{2}. $$ If $\mbox{gn}(C_n,s)=n/2$, then we must have equality throughout, which means that $h(i)=1$ for all $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain Lemmas 2.7-2.9: gn $=H(X)=\frac12 H_1^n\le\frac12\sum h(i)\le n/2$; equality forces $h(i)=1$.

nodes.name: Guessing number of cycles tends to $n/2$
nodes.statement: This same paper also shows that the limit of $\mbox{gn}(C_n,s) \to n/2$ as $s \rightarrow \infty$.

nodes.name: Fixed-number lower bound for non-square colour numbers
nodes.statement: If $n$ is odd and $s = m^2-t$ for integers $m$ and $t \geq 0$ then there exists a protocol $\mathcal{P}$ on $C_n$ with $s$ colours such that $$ \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \geq s^{n/2} \left( 1 - \frac{tn}{s} \right). $$
assumptions: $n$ is odd
$s = m^2-t$ for integers $m$ and $t \geq 0$
conclusions: there exists a protocol $\mathcal{P}$ on $C_n$ with $s$ colours such that $$ \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \geq s^{n/2} \left( 1 - \frac{tn}{s} \right). $$
nodes.statement_short: For odd $n$ and $s=m^2-t$, some protocol fixes at least $s^{n/2}(1-tn/s)$ colourings.
nodes.label: thm:round_up

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.5
nodes.statement: Consider the protocol $\mathcal{P}^\prime = \mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ on $C_n$ with $s^\prime = m^2$ colours and let $X^\prime \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:n/2}, we must have $H(X_i^\prime)=1$ and therefore $X_i^\prime$ is uniformly distributed over $\mathbb{Z}_{s^\prime}$ for all $i$. By the union bound, $$ \mathbb{P}\left( X_i^\prime<s \; \forall \: i \right) \geq 1 - \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{P}(X_i^\prime \geq s) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{t}{m^2} = 1 - \frac{tn}{m^2}. $$ Now, let $\mathcal{P}$ be a protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours such that $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$ for all colourings $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime)$ such that $c_i < s$ for all $i$ (such a protocol must exist by Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}). For this protocol, \begin{align*} \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) & \geq \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime) \: \mathbb{P}\left( X_i^\prime<s \; \forall \: i \right) \\ & \geq \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime) \left( 1 - \frac{tn}{m^2} \right) \\ & = (s+t)^{n/2} \left( 1 - tn(s+t)^{-1} \right) \\ & \geq s^{n/2} \left( 1 - \frac{tn}{s} \right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Run $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ with $m^2$ colours, union-bound the chance a fixed colouring uses a colour $\ge s$, and restrict via Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Convergence rate of $\mathrm{gn}(C_n,s)$ to $n/2$
nodes.statement: If $n \geq 4$ then $\mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = \frac{n}{2} - \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{s}\log_es} \right)$ as $s \rightarrow \infty$.
assumptions: $n \geq 4$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.6
nodes.statement: For even $n$ we have $\mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = \frac{n}{2}$. For odd $n$, let $m$ be the smallest positive integer such that $m^2 \geq s$. This gives $t = m^2-s = \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{s})$. If $\mathcal{P}$ is the protocol constructed in Theorem~\ref{thm:round_up}, then $$ \mbox{gn}(C_n,s) \geq \log_s\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \geq \frac{n}{2} + \log_s \left( 1 - \frac{tn}{s} \right) = \frac{n}{2} - \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{n}{\sqrt{s}\log_es} \right). $$
nodes.statement_short: Even $n$ is exact; for odd $n$ take $m^2\ge s$ minimal so $t=O(\sqrt s)$ and apply Theorem 3.5.

nodes.name: Flat function, semi-perfect function
nodes.statement: For any $z \in \mathbb{Z}_s$ and for any function $f : \mathbb{Z}_s^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_s$ let $f^{-1}(z) = \{ (x,y) \: | \: f(x,y)=z \}$. The function $f$ is called \emph{flat} if and only if $|f^{-1}(z)| = s$ for all $z$. Let $U = (U_1,U_2) \in_u \mathbb{Z}_s^2$. A \emph{semi-perfect} function, $f$, is any flat function such that the $U_1$ and $U_2$ are conditionally independent given $f(U)$ (Definition~\ref{defn:entropy}), \emph{i.e.} $$ I(U_1;U_2 \: | \: f(U)) = 0. $$
differentia: the $U_1$ and $U_2$ are conditionally independent given $f(U)$
nodes.statement_short: $f:\mathbb{Z}_s^2\to\mathbb{Z}_s$ is flat if every fibre has size $s$, semi-perfect if also $I(U_1;U_2|f(U))=0$ for uniform $U$.
nodes.label: defn:semi-perfect_function

nodes.name: $(k,\epsilon)$-uniform random variable
nodes.statement: For any positive integer $k$ and any $\epsilon >0$, a random variable $Y$ is called $(k,\epsilon)$-uniform if $Y$ takes values in a finite set $\mathcal{Y}$ with $|\mathcal{Y}| = k$ and, for any $y \in \mathcal{Y}$, $$ \left| \mathbb{P}(Y=y) - \frac{1}{k} \right| \leq \epsilon .$$
differentia: $Y$ takes values in a finite set $\mathcal{Y}$ with $|\mathcal{Y}| = k$
nodes.label: defn:(k,e)-uniform

nodes.name: Near-maximal entropy implies near-uniformity
nodes.statement: For any integer $k \geq 2$, any integer $s \geq 2$ and any $\epsilon >0$, there exists $\delta >0$ such that, for any random variable $Y$ which takes $k$ distinct values, if $H(Y)$ is the entropy of $Y$ (base $s$), then $$ H(Y) \geq \log_s k - \delta \qquad \implies \qquad Y \mbox{ is $(k,\epsilon)$-uniform.} $$
assumptions: any integer $k \geq 2$, any integer $s \geq 2$ and any $\epsilon >0$
any random variable $Y$ which takes $k$ distinct values
nodes.statement_short: If a $k$-valued variable has entropy within $\delta$ of $\log_s k$, it is $(k,\epsilon)$-uniform.
nodes.label: prop:delta

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement: For each $k$, it suffices to show this for all small enough $\epsilon$. Assume $7k\epsilon < 1$. We prove the contrapositive: \begin{itemize} \item Suppose that $\mathbb{P}(Y=y) \geq \frac{1}{k} + \epsilon$ for at least one value $y$. Entropy is greatest when $Y$ is as uniformly distributed as possible. Therefore, \begin{align*} H(Y) & = - \sum_i \mathbb{P}(Y=i) \log_s \mathbb{P}(Y=i) \\ & \leq - \left( \tfrac{1}{k} + \epsilon \right) \log_s \left( \tfrac{1}{k}+\epsilon \right) - (k-1) \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \tfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} \right) \log_s \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \tfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} \right) \\ & = \log_s k - \left( \tfrac{1}{k} + \epsilon \right) \log_s( 1 + k\epsilon ) - \left( \tfrac{k-1}{k} - \epsilon \right) \log_s \left( 1 - \tfrac{k\epsilon}{k-1} \right). \intertext{Since $0 < k\epsilon < \frac{1}{7}$, we can use the identity, $-\log_s(1-\gamma) \leq (\gamma + \frac{5}{9}\gamma^2)\log_es$ (valid for $|\gamma| \leq 1/7$), to simplify this expression.} H(Y) & \leq \log_sk - \frac{k\epsilon^2}{9} \left( 4 - 5k\epsilon + \tfrac{4}{k-1} + \tfrac{5k\epsilon}{(k-1)^2} \right)\log_es \\ & \leq \log_sk - \frac{k\epsilon^2}{3}\log_es. \end{align*} \item Now suppose $\mathbb{P}(Y=y) \leq \frac{1}{k} - \epsilon$ for at least one value $y$. The entropy would be greatest when $Y$ is as uniformly distributed as possible. Therefore, \begin{align*} H(Y) & = - \sum_i \mathbb{P}(Y=i) \log_s \mathbb{P}(Y=i) \\ & \leq - \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \epsilon \right) \log_s \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \epsilon \right) -(k-1) \left( \tfrac{1}{k} + \tfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} \right) \log_s \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \tfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} \right) \\ & = \log_sk - \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \epsilon \right) \log_s ( 1 - k\epsilon ) - \left( \tfrac{k-1}{k} + \epsilon \right) \log_s \left( 1 + \tfrac{k\epsilon}{k-1} \right). \intertext{We can use the identity, $-\log_s(1-\gamma) \leq (\gamma + \frac{5}{9}\gamma^2)\log_es$, again to simplify this expression. } H(Y) & \leq \log_sk - \tfrac{k\epsilon^2}{9} \left( 4 - 5k\epsilon + \tfrac{4}{k-1} - \tfrac{5k\epsilon}{(k-1)^2} \right) \log_es\\ & \leq \log_sk - \frac{k\epsilon^2}{3}\log_es. \end{align*} \end{itemize} In either case, $H(Y) < \log_s k - \delta$ for any $\delta < \frac{k\epsilon^2}{3}\log_es$.
nodes.statement_short: Contrapositive: if some probability deviates by $\epsilon$, bound entropy by the most-uniform such distribution and a log Taylor estimate, giving deficit $k\epsilon^2\log_e s/3$.

nodes.name: Non-semi-perfect functions lose conditional mutual information
nodes.statement: For any integer $s \geq 2$, there exists positive constant $\epsilon = \epsilon(s)$ that satisfies the following property. For any non semi-perfect function $f : \mathbb{Z}_s^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_s$ and for any three $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform random variables $Y_1,Y_2,Y_3$ over $\mathbb{Z}_s$ satisfying $Y_2 = f(Y_1,Y_3)$, if $(Y_1,Y_3)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $$ I(Y_1;Y_3|Y_2) \geq \tfrac{1}{2} \min \big\{ I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) \; \big| \; f \mbox{ is a flat but not semi-perfect} \big\} = \delta_1,$$ where $U = (U_1,U_2) \in_u \mathbb{Z}_s^2$.
assumptions: any integer $s \geq 2$
any non semi-perfect function $f : \mathbb{Z}_s^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_s$
any three $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform random variables $Y_1,Y_2,Y_3$ over $\mathbb{Z}_s$ satisfying $Y_2 = f(Y_1,Y_3)$
$(Y_1,Y_3)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform
conclusions: there exists positive constant $\epsilon = \epsilon(s)$ that satisfies the following property
$$ I(Y_1;Y_3|Y_2) \geq \tfrac{1}{2} \min \big\{ I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) \; \big| \; f \mbox{ is a flat but not semi-perfect} \big\} = \delta_1,$$
nodes.statement_short: For near-uniform $Y_1,Y_2,Y_3$ with $Y_2=f(Y_1,Y_3)$ and $f$ not semi-perfect, $I(Y_1;Y_3|Y_2)\ge\delta_1(s)>0$.
nodes.label: lem:alpha

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement: The value $\delta_1=\delta_1(s) = \tfrac{1}{2} \min \big\{ I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) \; \big| \; f \mbox{ is a flat but not semi-perfect} \big\}$ is well-defined for any $s \geq 2$, because there are only a finite number of functions $f : \mathbb{Z}_s^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_s$, and at least one of them is flat and not semi-perfect hence we can take the minimum of these. For example, the function $f(x,y) = x+y$ (mod $s$) is flat but not semi-perfect. First, let $\epsilon < \frac{1}{s^2(s+2)}$, so that $$ \frac{1}{s^2} - (s-1)\epsilon > \frac{1}{s^2} - (s+1)\epsilon > \epsilon. $$ We show that $f$ is flat by contradiction. Since $(Y_1,Y_3)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform: \begin{itemize} \item If $| f^{-1}(z) | \geq s+1$ then $$ \mathbb{P}(Y_2=z) = \mathbb{P}( (Y_1,Y_3) \in f^{-1}(z)) \geq (s+1) \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - \epsilon \right) = \tfrac{1}{s} + \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - (s+1)\epsilon \right) > \tfrac{1}{s} + \epsilon. $$ \item If $| f^{-1}(z) | \leq s-1$ then $$ \mathbb{P}(Y_2=z) = \mathbb{P}( (Y_1,Y_3) \in f^{-1}(z)) \leq (s-1) \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} + \epsilon \right) = \tfrac{1}{s} - \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - (s-1)\epsilon \right) < \tfrac{1}{s} - \epsilon. $$ \end{itemize} Both cases contradict the assumption that $Y_2$ is $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform. Therefore $f$ is a flat function and so $$I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) \geq 2\delta_1.$$ Moreover, since $(Y_1,Y_3)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $U$ and $(Y_1,Y_3)$ differ in distribution by less than $\epsilon$. Since mutual information is continuous, we can choose $\epsilon$ small enough so that $$ \big| I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) - I(Y_1;Y_3|Y_2) \big| \leq \delta_1. $$ Then, by the triangle inequality, $I(Y_1;Y_3|Y_2) \geq \delta_1$.
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_1$ is a minimum over finitely many functions; near-uniformity forces $f$ flat, then continuity of mutual information transfers the bound. Key step: showing $f$ is flat by contradiction on fibre sizes.

nodes.name: Choice of $\epsilon$ and $\delta$
nodes.statement: From now on, for any integer $s \geq 2$, let $\epsilon = \epsilon(s) >0$ be chosen small enough so that $\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}$ and $\epsilon$ satisfies Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha}. Then let $\delta_2 = \delta_2(s) >0$ be chosen small enough to satisfy Proposition~\ref{prop:delta} for both $k=s$ and $k=s^2$ for this value $\epsilon$. Then, with $\delta_1$ as defined in Lemma \ref{lem:alpha}, let $\delta= \min (\delta_1,\delta_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\epsilon(s)\le 1/(s^2(2s+1))$ satisfying Lemma 4.4, $\delta_2$ from Proposition 4.3 for $k=s,s^2$, and $\delta=\min(\delta_1,\delta_2)$.
nodes.label: defn:epsilon,delta

nodes.name: Shannon-type bound on $H_1^5$
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 5$ be an integer and let $\mathcal{P}$ be any non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours. The random variables $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5$ (Definition~\ref{defn:C_n}) satisfy: $$ H_1^5 \leq 3+h(2,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3). $$
assumptions: $n \geq 5$ be an integer
$\mathcal{P}$ be any non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours
nodes.label: lem:shannon

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:H(X),h(i)}, it suffices to show $H_1^5 \leq h(1)+h(3)+h(5)+h(2,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3)$. By Shannon's Inequality (Proposition~\ref{prop:known_entropy_results}) we have: \begin{align} h(2,3,4) + h(3) & = h(2,3) + h(3,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3), \\ h(1,2,3,4) + h(2,3) & \leq h(1,2,3) + h(2,3,4), \\ \mbox{and} \quad h(2,3,4,5) + h(3,4) & \leq h(2,3,4) + h(3,4,5). \\ \intertext{Also, since $X_i = f_i(X_{i-1},X_{i+1})$ for $i=2,3,4$ respectively we have:} h(1,2,3) &= h(1,3) \leq h(1) + h(3), \\ h(2,3,4) & = h(2,4), \\ \mbox{and} \quad h(3,4,5) &= h(3,5) \leq h(3) + h(5). \end{align} The required result is the sum of equations (\ref{eq:mutual_information}), (\ref{eq:shannon12}), (\ref{eq:shannon23}), (\ref{eq:func1}), (\ref{eq:func2}) and (\ref{eq:func3}).
nodes.statement_short: Sum Shannon inequalities (4.1)-(4.3) and determinism identities (4.4)-(4.6).

nodes.name: Determinism of $X_4$
nodes.statement: \mbox{and} \quad h(3,4,5) &= h(3,5) \leq h(3) + h(5).
nodes.label: eq:func3

nodes.name: One non-semi-perfect function bounds $H_j^{j+4}$
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 5$ be an integer and let $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be a non-trivial protocal on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and let $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$. For any $j$, if $f_{j+2}$ is not semi-perfect or $(X_{j+1},X_{j+3})$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform then $H_j^{j+4} \leq 5 - \delta$, for $\delta$ as in Definition \ref{defn:epsilon,delta}.
assumptions: $n \geq 5$ be an integer
$\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be a non-trivial protocal on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and let $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$
$f_{j+2}$ is not semi-perfect or $(X_{j+1},X_{j+3})$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform
nodes.label: lem:one_non-semi-perfect_function

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality let $j=1$. There are $3$ cases. \begin{itemize} \item If, for any $i \in \{ 1,2,3,4,5 \}$, the variable $X_i$ is not $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $h(i) \leq 1 - \delta_2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:delta}). In this case, by Lemma~\ref{lem:H_j^k<sum(h(i))}, $$ H_1^5 \leq \sum_{i=1}^5 h(i) \leq 5 - \delta_2. $$ \item If $(X_2,X_4)$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $h(2,4) \leq 2-\delta_2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:delta}). Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{lem:shannon}, we have $$ H_1^5 \leq 3 + h(2,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3) \leq 5-\delta_2. $$ \item Otherwise, $X_2,X_3,X_4$ are each $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform and $(X_2,X_4)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform and $f_3$ is not semi-perfect. In this case, by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha}, we have $I(X_{j+1};X_{j+3}|X_{j+2}) \geq \delta_1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:shannon}, we have $$ H_1^5 \leq 3 + h(2,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3) \leq 5-\delta_1. $$ \end{itemize} In all cases, we have $H_1^5 \leq 5 - \delta$ because $\delta = \min\{ \delta_1 , \delta_2 \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Three cases: a non-uniform marginal, a non-uniform pair, or a non-semi-perfect $f_3$; each loses $\delta$ via Prop. 4.3, Lemma 4.6 or Lemma 4.4.

nodes.name: Bound on $H_j^{j+6}$ near a non-semi-perfect function
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 7$ be an integer and let $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and let $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$. For any $j$, if any of $f_{j+2}$, $f_{j+3}$ or $f_{j+4}$ are not semi-perfect, or any of $(X_{j+1},X_{j+3})$, $(X_{j+2},X_{j+4})$ or $(X_{j+3},X_{j+5})$ are not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $H_{j}^{j+6} \leq 7 - \delta$.
assumptions: $n \geq 7$ be an integer
$\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and let $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$
any of $f_{j+2}$, $f_{j+3}$ or $f_{j+4}$ are not semi-perfect, or any of $(X_{j+1},X_{j+3})$, $(X_{j+2},X_{j+4})$ or $(X_{j+3},X_{j+5})$ are not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform
nodes.label: lem:at_least_one_non-semi-perfect_function

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.8
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality let $j=1$. We treat each case individually, and use Lemma~\ref{lem:one_non-semi-perfect_function}. \begin{itemize} \item If $f_3$ is not semi-perfect or $(X_2,X_4)$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform then \begin{align*} H_1^7 & = h(1,2,3,4,5,6) + h(2,3,4,5,6,7) \\ & = h(1,2,3,4,6) + h(2,3,4,5,7) \\ & \leq H_1^5 + h(6) + h(7) \\ & \leq (5 - \delta) + 1 + 1. \end{align*} \item If $f_4$ is not semi-perfect or $(X_3,X_5)$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform then \begin{align*} H_1^7 & = h(1,2,3,4,5,6) + h(2,3,4,5,6,7) \\ & = h(1,3,4,5,6) + h(2,3,4,5,7) \\ & \leq h(1) + H_2^6 + h(7) \\ & \leq 1 + (5 - \delta) + 1. \end{align*} \item If $f_5$ is not semi-perfect or $(X_4,X_6)$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform then \begin{align*} H_1^7 & = h(1,2,3,4,5,6) + h(2,3,4,5,6,7) \\ & = h(1,3,4,5,6) + h(2,4,5,6,7) \\ & \leq h(1) + h(2) + H_3^7 \\ & \leq 1 + 1 + (5 - \delta). \end{align*} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Case on which window holds the defect; drop determined indices and apply Lemma 4.7 to the 5-window plus $h(i)\le1$ for the rest.

nodes.name: Many non-semi-perfect windows force a small fixed number
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 7(\delta^{-1}+2)$. Suppose $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ is a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and let $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$ such that, for each $j$, either \begin{itemize} \item at least one of $f_{j-1}$, $f_j$, $f_{j+1}$ is not semi-perfect, or \item at least one of $(X_{j-2},X_j)$, $(X_{j-1},X_{j+1})$, $(X_j,X_{j+2})$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, \end{itemize} then $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) < s^{(n-1)/2}$.
assumptions: $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ is a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours and let $X\in_u \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$
at least one of $f_{j-1}$, $f_j$, $f_{j+1}$ is not semi-perfect
at least one of $(X_{j-2},X_j)$, $(X_{j-1},X_{j+1})$, $(X_j,X_{j+2})$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform
nodes.label: lem:many_non-semi-perfect_functions

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.9
nodes.statement: Let $m$ be an odd integer such that $m > \delta^{-1}$ and $7m \leq n$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:H(X)=sum(H)} and Lemma~\ref{lem:at_least_one_non-semi-perfect_function}, we have \begin{align*} 2H(X) & \leq \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} H_{7j+1}^{7j+7} + \sum_{i=7m}^{n-1} h(i) \\ & \leq m(7 - \delta) + (n-7m) \\ & = n - m \delta. \end{align*} Since $m > \delta^{-1}$, this means that $H(X) < \frac{n-1}{2}$. Therefore $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) < s^{(n-1)/2}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:H(X),h(i)}.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $2H(X)$ into $m>\delta^{-1}$ windows of length 7 via Lemma 2.9, each losing $\delta$ by Lemma 4.8.

nodes.name: Perfect function
nodes.statement: For any function $f: \mathbb{Z}_s^2 \to \mathbb{Z}$, let $L(f,z)$ and $R(f,z)$ denote the subsets \begin{align*} L(f,z) & = \{ x \: | \: f(x,y)=z \mbox{ for some } y \} \\ \mbox{and} \quad R(f,z) & = \{ y \: | \: f(x,y)=z \mbox{ for some } x \}. \end{align*} The function $f$ is called a \emph{perfect} function if it is semi-perfect and the cardinalities $|L(f,z)|$ and $|R(f,z)|$ do not depend on $z$, \emph{i.e.} if $|L(f,z)|=|L(f,z^\prime)|$ and $|R(f,z)|=|R(z^\prime)|$ for all $z,z^\prime \in \mathbb{Z}_s$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
differentia: the cardinalities $|L(f,z)|$ and $|R(f,z)|$ do not depend on $z$
nodes.statement_short: A semi-perfect $f$ whose left and right projections $L(f,z)$, $R(f,z)$ of each fibre have sizes independent of $z$.
nodes.label: defn:perfect_function

nodes.name: Fibres of semi-perfect functions are rectangles
nodes.statement: If $f$ is a semi-perfect function then for all $z \in \mathbb{Z}_s$ then $$ f^{-1}(z) = L(f,z) \times R(f,z). $$ Moreover $|L(f,z)||R(f,z)| = s$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
assumptions: $f$ is a semi-perfect function
conclusions: for all $z \in \mathbb{Z}_s$ then $$ f^{-1}(z) = L(f,z) \times R(f,z). $$
nodes.label: prop:LR=s

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.2
nodes.statement: Let $U = (U_1,U_2) \in_u \mathbb{Z}_s^2$ and for a given $z$, let $L = L(f,z)$ and $R = R(f,z)$. Since $f$ is semi-perfect, we have $I(U_1,U_2 \; | \; f(U))=0$. Therefore, $U_1$ and $U_2$ are conditionally independent given $f(U)$. For any $x \in L$ and any $y \in R$, we must have \begin{align*}& \mathbb{P}(U_1=x \wedge U_2=y | f(U)=z) = \mathbb{P}(U_1=x | f(U)=z)\mathbb{P}(U_2=y | f(U)=z) > 0, \\ &\mbox{and }f^{-1}(z) = L \times R.\end{align*} Furthermore, since $U_1$ and $U_2$ are independently uniformly distributed over $\mathbb{Z}_s$ and $U$ is uniformly distributed over $\mathbb{Z}_s^2$, we have $$ \frac{1}{s} = \mathbb{P}( f(U)=z) = \mathbb{P}( U_1 \in L \wedge U_2 \in R) = \mathbb{P}( U_1 \in L) \times \mathbb{P}(U_2 \in R) = \frac{|L|}{s} \times \frac{|R|}{s}. $$ Therefore, $|L||R| = s$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
nodes.statement_short: Conditional independence given $f(U)$ makes each fibre a product $L\times R$; uniformity gives $|L||R|=s$.

nodes.name: Two adjacent semi-perfect functions have matching fibre sizes
nodes.statement: Let $s \geq 2$ be an integer, let $0 <\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}$ be a constant. Let $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be any non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours and let $X \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$. If $f_1$ and $f_2$ are semi-perfect functions and $(X_0,X_2)$ and $(X_1,X_3)$ are $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, then, for any $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{Z}_s$, we have $$ | \{ c_0 | f_1(c_0,c_2)=c_1 \} | = | \{ c_3 | f_2(c_1,c_3)=c_2 \} |. $$
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
assumptions: $s \geq 2$ be an integer
$0 <\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}$ be a constant
$\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be any non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours and let $X \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$
$f_1$ and $f_2$ are semi-perfect functions and $(X_0,X_2)$ and $(X_1,X_3)$ are $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform
nodes.label: lem:two_semi-perfect_functions

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: We proceed by contradiction. Let $S_0 = \{ c_0 | f_1(c_0,c_2)=c_1 \}$ and $S_3 = \{ c_3 | f_2(c_1,c_3)=c_2 \}$. Without loss of generality assume $|S_0|<|S_3|$ so since $|S_0| < s$ we must have $|S_3| > \left( 1 + \frac{1}{s} \right)|S_0|$. Now since $(X_0,X_2)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, $$ \mathbb{P}( X_1=c_1 \wedge X_2=c_2) = \sum_{x \in S_0} \mathbb{P}\big( (X_0,X_2) = (x,c_2) \big) \leq |S_0| \left( \frac{1}{s^2} + \epsilon \right). $$ Similarly, since $(X_1,X_3)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, $$ \mathbb{P}( X_1=c_1 \wedge X_2=c_2) = \sum_{x \in S_3}\mathbb{P}\big( (X_1,X_3) = (c_1,x) \big) \geq |S_3| \left( \frac{1}{s^2} - \epsilon \right). $$ However, since $\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}$, this implies $$ 1 + \frac{1}{s} < \frac{|S_3|}{|S_0|} \leq \frac{s^{-2}+\epsilon}{s^{-2}-\epsilon} \leq \frac{\frac{1}{s^2}+\frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}}{\frac{1}{s^2}-\frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}} = 1 + \frac{1}{s}, $$ which is a contradiction.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: compute $\mathbb{P}(X_1=c_1,X_2=c_2)$ via both uniform pairs; unequal fibre sizes contradict $\epsilon\le 1/(s^2(2s+1))$.

nodes.name: Three semi-perfect functions force a perfect function
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours, let $X \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$ and let $j$ be any index (indices taken modulo $n$). If $f_{j-1}$, $f_j$ and $f_{j+1}$ are semi-perfect functions and $(X_{j-2},X_j)$, $(X_{j-1},X_{j+1})$ and $(X_j,X_{j+2})$ are $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $f_j$ is a perfect function.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
assumptions: $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours, let $X \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$ and let $j$ be any index (indices taken modulo $n$)
$f_{j-1}$, $f_j$ and $f_{j+1}$ are semi-perfect functions and $(X_{j-2},X_j)$, $(X_{j-1},X_{j+1})$ and $(X_j,X_{j+2})$ are $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform
nodes.label: lem:three_semi-perfect_functions

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: We proceed by contradiction. Without loss of generality, assume $j=0$ and fix $c_0,c_0^\prime \in \mathbb{Z}_s$ arbitrarily. Now choose $c_{-1},c_1\in \mathbb{Z}_s$ such that $f_0(c_{-1},c_1)=c_0$ and choose $c_{-1}^\prime,c_1^\prime \in \mathbb{Z}_s$ such that $f_0(c_{-1}^\prime ,c_1^\prime)=c_0^\prime$. Also let $c_0^{\prime\prime} = f_0(c_{-1}^\prime ,c_1)$. Now by Lemma~\ref{lem:two_semi-perfect_functions}, \begin{align*} |L(f_0,c_0)| = | \{ x | f_0(x,c_1)=c_0 \} | = | \{ x | f_1(c_0,x)=c_1 \} | & = |R(f_1,c_1)| \\ \mbox{and} \qquad |L(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})| = | \{ x | f_0(x,c_1)=c_0^{\prime\prime} \} | = | \{ x | f_1(c_0^{\prime\prime},x)=c_1 \} | & = |R(f_1,c_1)|. \end{align*} Similarly \begin{align*} |R(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})| = | \{ x | f_0(c_{-1}^{\prime},x)=c_0^{\prime\prime} \} | = | \{ x | f_{-1}(x,c_0^{\prime\prime})=c_{-1}^{\prime} \} | & = |L(f_{-1},c_{-1}^{\prime})| \\ \mbox{and} \qquad |R(f_0,c_0^{\prime})| = | \{ x | f_0(c_{-1}^{\prime},x)=c_0^{\prime} \} | = | \{ x | f_{-1}(x,c_0^{\prime})=c_{-1}^{\prime} \} | & = |L(f_{-1},c_{-1}^{\prime})|. \end{align*} Recall that $|L(f_0,z)|\cdot |R(f_0,z)|=s$ for all $z\in \mathbb{Z}_s$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:LR=s}). Therefore, $|R(f_0,c_0^{\prime})|=|R(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})|$ if and only if $|L(f_0,c_0^{\prime})|=|L(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})|$. Hence, $$ |L(f_0,c_0)| = |L(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})| = |L(f_0,c_0^{\prime})|. $$ Similarly, $|R(f_0,c_0)| = |R(f_0,c_0^\prime)|$ (for arbitrary $c_0,c_0^\prime \in \mathbb{Z}_s$) and therefore $f_0$ is a perfect function.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma 5.3 on both neighbours to equate $|L(f_0,\cdot)|$ and $|R(f_0,\cdot)|$ across values via an intermediate $c_0''$, with $|L||R|=s$.

nodes.name: A perfect function caps the fixed number
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours, such that $f_j$ is a perfect function for some $j$. Then $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \leq as^{(n-1)/2}$, where $a$ is the greatest factor of $s$ less than or equal to $\sqrt{s}$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
assumptions: $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be a non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s \geq 2$ colours, such that $f_j$ is a perfect function for some $j$
$a$ is the greatest factor of $s$ less than or equal to $\sqrt{s}$
nodes.label: lem:one_perfect_function

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, assume $j=2$. Since $f_2$ is perfect, let $l = |L(f_2,z)|$ and $r=|R(f_2,z)|$. Without loss of generality, assume $l \leq r$ and therefore $l \leq a$. Then $X_2$ takes at most $s$ different values and $X_1$, conditioned on $X_2=z$ for any $z \in \mathbb{Z}_s$, takes at most $l$ different values. Therefore, the pair $(X_1,X_2)$ takes at most $ls$ different values in $\mathbb{Z}_s^2$ and $h(1,2) \leq \log_s(ls)$. We have \begin{align*} H(X) & = h(1,2,3, \ldots ,n) \\ & = h(1,2,4,6, \ldots ,n-3,n-1) \\ & \leq h(1,2) + \sum_{i=1}^{(n-3)/2} h(2i+2) \\ & \leq \log_s(ls) + \frac{n-3}{2}. \end{align*} Therefore $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) = s^{H(X)} \leq ls^{(n-1)/2} \leq as^{(n-1)/2}$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
nodes.statement_short: With $l=|L(f_2,z)|\le a$, $(X_1,X_2)$ takes at most $ls$ values; bound $H(X)$ by $h(1,2)$ plus single entropies of even vertices.

nodes.name: Guessing number of large odd cycles
nodes.statement: For any integer $s \geq 2$, let $a$ be the greatest factor of $s$ less than or equal to $\sqrt{s}$. There exists some $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $$\mbox{gn} (C_n,s)=\begin{cases} \frac{n}{2}, &\mbox{for even } n , \\ \frac{n-1}{2}+\log_s a, &\mbox{for odd }n>N, \end{cases}$$ and $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ is an optimal protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours for any odd $n \geq N$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
assumptions: any integer $s \geq 2$
$a$ be the greatest factor of $s$ less than or equal to $\sqrt{s}$
conclusions: There exists some $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $$\mbox{gn} (C_n,s)=\begin{cases} \frac{n}{2}, &\mbox{for even } n , \\ \frac{n-1}{2}+\log_s a, &\mbox{for odd }n>N, \end{cases}$$
$\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ is an optimal protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours for any odd $n \geq N$
nodes.statement_short: For fixed $s$ and all large odd $n$, gn$(C_n,s)=(n-1)/2+\log_s a$ with $a$ the largest factor $\le\sqrt s$, attained by $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$.
also_stated_at: Our main result in Theorem~\ref{thm:n_large} states that, for any given $s$, this fractional-clique-partition protocol is optimal on any large enough odd cycle.
In this section, we prove our main result in Theorem~\ref{thm:n_large}, which states that, for any given $s$, this fractional-clique-partition protocol is optimal on any large enough odd cycle.
nodes.label: thm:n_large

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.6
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ be the values given in Definition~\ref{defn:epsilon,delta}, let $N = 7(\delta^{-1}+2)$ and let $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be any non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours. We have two cases: \begin{description} \item[Case one] For all $j$, either: \begin{itemize} \item at least one of the functions $f_{j-1}$, $f_j$ and $f_{j+1}$ is not semi-perfect or \item at least one of $(X_{j-2},X_j)$, $(X_{j-1},X_{j+1})$, $(X_j,X_{j+2})$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform. \end{itemize} \item[Case two] There exists some $j$ such that: \begin{itemize} \item the functions $f_{j-1}$, $f_j$ and $f_{j+1}$ are all semi-perfect and \item $(X_{j-2},X_j)$, $(X_{j-1},X_{j+1})$ and $(X_j,X_{j+2})$ are all $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform. \end{itemize} \end{description} For case one, we can conclude that $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \leq s^{(n-1)/2} \leq \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:many_non-semi-perfect_functions}. In case two, $f_j$ must be a perfect function (Lemma~\ref{lem:three_semi-perfect_functions}) and then $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \leq as^{(n-1)/2} = \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:one_perfect_function}). In either case, $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp}) \geq \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$. Hence $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ is optimal.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles
nodes.statement_short: Case split: either every window has a non-semi-perfect or non-uniform part (Lemma 4.9), or some $f_j$ is perfect (Lemmas 5.4, 5.5); both give fix$\le$ fix$(\mathcal{P}_{fcp})$.

nodes.name: Index coding with side information
nodes.statement: In the problem of index coding with side information on a graph $G$, a sender aims communicate $n$ messages $c_1,c_2, \ldots ,c_n$ (where $c_i \in \mathbb{Z}_s$) to $n$ receivers $v_1,v_2, \ldots ,v_n$ (the vertices of $G$). Each receiver, $c_i$, knows $c_j$ in advance, for each $j$ such that $v_iv_j$ is an edge in $G$. The sender is required to broadcast a message to all receivers (the same message to all receivers) so that each receiver, $v_i$, can recover $c_i$.
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information
nodes.origin_citation: Alon et al. 2008; Bar-Yossef et al. 2011
nodes.statement_short: A sender broadcasts one common message so each receiver $v_i$, knowing its neighbours' messages, recovers $c_i$.

nodes.name: Information defect
nodes.statement: If $m$ is the smallest integer such that the sender can achieve this by broadcasting one of only $m$ different messages, then the \emph{information defect} \cite{Riis2007graph} of $G$ with $s$ colours is defined to be $$ \beta(G,s) = \log_s(m). $$
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information

nodes.name: Confusion graph
nodes.statement: Explicitly, let $\mathfrak{C} _s(G)$ be the \emph{confusion graph} \cite{Alon2008broadcasting,bar2011index} (also known as the ``code graph'' \cite{Christofides2011guessing}), defined to have vertex set $\mathbb{Z}_s^n$, in which two vertices $c,c' \in \mathbb{Z}_s^n$ are adjacent if and only if for some $i \in [n]$, $c_i \neq c_i^\prime$ but for each $j$ such that $ij \in E(G)$ we have $c_j=c_j^\prime$.
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information
nodes.origin_citation: Alon et al. 2008; Bar-Yossef et al. 2011
nodes.statement_short: Graph on $\mathbb{Z}_s^n$ joining colourings that differ at some $i$ while agreeing on all neighbours of $i$.

nodes.name: Information defect and guessing number via the confusion graph
nodes.statement: If $\chi(\mathfrak{C}_s(G))$ is chromatic number of the confusion graph of $G$ and $\alpha(\mathfrak{C}_s(G))$ is the size of the largest independent set in the confusion graph of $G$, then $$ \beta(G,s) = \log_s \chi(\mathfrak{C}_s(G)) \qquad \mbox{and} \qquad \mbox{gn}(G,s) = \log_s \alpha(\mathfrak{C}_s(G)). $$
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information
assumptions: $\chi(\mathfrak{C}_s(G))$ is chromatic number of the confusion graph of $G$ and $\alpha(\mathfrak{C}_s(G))$ is the size of the largest independent set in the confusion graph of $G$

nodes.name: Information defect plus guessing number is at least $n$
nodes.statement: For any graph $H$, we have the identity $\chi(H)\alpha(H) \geq |H|$ and so we have the identity \cite{Riis2007graph} $$ \beta(G,s) + \mbox{gn}(G,s) \geq \log_s \left| \mathfrak{C}_s(G) \right| = n. $$
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information
assumptions: any graph $H$

nodes.name: Information defect of large odd cycles
nodes.statement: For a given $s$, let $b$ be the smallest factor of $s$ which is at least $\sqrt{s}$. There exists some $N$ such that for all odd $n>N$, $$ \beta(C_n,s) = \frac{n-1}{2} + \log_sb. $$
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information
assumptions: a given $s$
$b$ be the smallest factor of $s$ which is at least $\sqrt{s}$
conclusions: There exists some $N$ such that for all odd $n>N$, $$ \beta(C_n,s) = \frac{n-1}{2} + \log_sb. $$
nodes.label: thm:defective

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.1
nodes.statement: Write $a=s/b$. First by Theorem~\ref{thm:n_large}, $\mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = (n-1)/2 +\log_sa$ for all large enough odd $n$. Therefore, $$ \beta(C_n,s) \geq n - \mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = \frac{n-1}{2} + \log_sb. $$ To show that we in fact get equality, we define a set of $bs^{(n-1)/2}$ possible messages with which the sender can solve the index coding with side information problem on $C_n$. Let $\phi$ and $\psi$ be defined as in Definition~\ref{defn:phi_and_psi}. This means that $\phi \times \psi$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{Z}_a \times \mathbb{Z}_b$ to $\mathbb{Z}_s$. Now for any colouring $c = (c_1,c_2, \ldots ,c_n) \in \mathbb{Z}_s^n$ let the sender broadcast the following values: \begin{itemize} \item For $i=1,2,3, \ldots ,\tfrac{n-1}{2}$, the sender broadcasts the residue $\phi(c_{2i-1})+\phi(c_{2i})$ modulo $a$ and the residue $\psi(c_{2i})+\psi(c_{2i+1})$ modulo $b$. \item Additionally, the sender broadcasts the residue $\psi(c_1)+\phi(c_n)$ modulo $b$. \end{itemize} The sender broadcasts $\frac{n-1}{2}$ residues modulo $a$ and $\frac{n+1}{2}$ residues modulo $b$, and so the total number of possible messages that the sender might send is $$ m = a^{(n-1)/2}b^{(n+1)/2} = bs^{(n-1)/2}. $$ Furthermore, each receiver, $v_i$, knows $c_{i-1}$ and $c_{i+1}$, and so can recover both $c_i$ because she can recover both $\phi(c_i)$ and $\psi(c_i)$.
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound from Theorem 5.6 and $\beta+$gn$\ge n$; upper bound by an explicit code broadcasting coordinate-wise pair sums modulo $a$ and $b$.

nodes.name: Define $\mathcal{P}'$ componentwise
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots f_n)$ then define $\mathcal{P}^\prime = (f_1^\prime,f_2^\prime, \ldots ,f_n^\prime )$ in the following way.

nodes.name: Keep $f_i$ when all colours are below $s'$
nodes.statement: If $0 \leq c_j<s^\prime$ for all $j$ such that $v_iv_j \in E$, and $0 \leq f_i(c)<s^\prime$ then $f_i^\prime(c) = f_i(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Keep $f_i$ when all colours are below $s'$

nodes.name: Guess 0 otherwise
nodes.statement: If $s^\prime \leq c_j < s$ for any $j$ such that $v_iv_j \in E$, or $s^\prime \leq f_i(c) < s$ then $f_i^\prime(c) = 0$.

nodes.name: Fixed colourings with small colours stay fixed
nodes.statement: For any colouring $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$, if $0 \leq c_i < s^\prime$ for all $i$, then $\mathcal{P}^\prime(c) = \mathcal{P}(c) = c$ so $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed colourings with small colours stay fixed

nodes.name: Bound $h(i)\le1$ by the uniform maximum
nodes.statement: The entropy of any random variable over a finite domain is maximised when the variable is uniformly distributed. Therefore, $h(i) = H(X_i) \leq H(U)$ where $U$ is a random variable uniformly distributed over $\mathbb{Z}_s$. Hence, $$ h(i) \leq H(U) = - \sum \frac{1}{s} \log_s \frac{1}{s} = 1. $$

nodes.name: Compute $H(X)=\log_s$ fix
nodes.statement: The variable $X$ is uniformly distributed over $\mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$. Therefore, $$ H(X) = - \sum \frac{1}{\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})} \log_s \frac{1}{\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})} = \log_s \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}). $$

nodes.name: Set up induction on $k-j$
nodes.statement: We prove this by induction on $(k-j)$. Recall that $h(i_1,i_2,i_3, \ldots ) = H(X_{i_1},X_{i_2},X_{i_3}, \ldots )$.

nodes.name: Base case $k=j+3$
nodes.statement: {\bf Base case: }$k=j+3$. Since $X_{j+1} = f_{j+1}(X_j,X_{j+2})$ and $X_{j+2} = f_{j+2}(X_{j+1},X_{j+3})$ we have \begin{align*} h(j,j+1,j+2) = h(j,j+2) & \leq h(j)+h(j+2) \\ \mbox{and} \qquad h(j+1,j+2,j+3) = h(j+1,j+3) & \leq h(j+1)+h(j+3) , \end{align*} respectively. Adding these together yields: $$ H_j^{j+3} = h(j,j+1,j+2) + h(j+1,j+2,j+3) \leq h(j)+h(j+1)+h(j+2)+h(j+3). $$

nodes.name: Inductive step via nonnegative conditional mutual informatio
nodes.statement: {\bf Inductive step:} $k \geq j+4$. Since $X_{k-1} = f_{k-1}(X_{k-2},X_k)$ we have \begin{align*} h(j+1,j+2, \ldots ,k) & = h(j+1,j+2, \ldots ,k-2,k) \\ & \leq h(j+1,j+2, \ldots ,k-2)+h(k). \end{align*} By Proposition~\ref{prop:known_entropy_results}, $ I(X_j ; X_{k-1} | X_{j+1},X_{j+2}, \ldots ,X_{k-2})\geq 0$. Adding these together yields $$ H_j^k \leq H_j^{k-1} + h(k). $$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via nonnegative conditional mutual information

nodes.name: Set up induction on $k$
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $k$.

nodes.name: Base case $k=2$
nodes.statement: {\bf Base case:} $k=2$. Since $X_1 = f_1(X_n,X_2)$ and $X_n = f_n(X_{n-1},X_1)$, we have $$ H(X) = h(2,3,4, \ldots ,n) \qquad \mbox{and} \qquad H(X) = h(1,2,3, \ldots ,n-1) ,$$ respectively. Adding these together gives $H_1^n = 2H(X) = 2\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$.

nodes.name: Inductive step via Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: {\bf Inductive step.} By Proposition \ref{prop:H=sum(H)}, for any $d(k-1)+2 \leq d(k) \leq n-2$, we have $$ H_{d(k-1)+1}^{n} = H_{d(k-1)+1}^{d(k)} + H_{d(k)+1}^{n}. $$

nodes.name: Count fixed colourings
nodes.statement: Let $n = 2k+1$. We count the number of colourings of $C_n$ for which the protocol $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ guesses correctly.

nodes.name: Count copying pairs: $a^kb^k$
nodes.statement: For any colouring $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp})$, there are $k$ pairs of vertices copying each other's first coordinates and there are $a$ different choices for $\phi$ for each pair. Similarly, for each of the $k$ pairs of vertices copying each other's second coordinates, there are $b$ different choices for $\psi$. This yields $a^kb^k$ possibilities.

nodes.name: Extra factor $a$ from the $v_1$--$v_n$ link
nodes.statement: Additionally, the first coordinate of vertex $v_n$ must equal the second coordinate of vertex $v_1$, for which there are $a$ possible colours.

nodes.name: Multiply to get $as^{(n-1)/2}$
nodes.statement: Multiplying these together yields $$ \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp}) = a^{k+1}b^k = as^{(n-1)/2}. $$

nodes.name: Chain Lemmas 2.7-2.9
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be an optimal protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:H(X),h(i)},~\ref{lem:H_j^k<sum(h(i))} and ~\ref{lem:H(X)=sum(H)}, we have $$ \mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = \log_s\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) = H(X) = \tfrac{1}{2} H_1^n \leq \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n h(i) \leq \frac{n}{2}. $$

nodes.name: Equality case forces $h(i)=1$
nodes.statement: If $\mbox{gn}(C_n,s)=n/2$, then we must have equality throughout, which means that $h(i)=1$ for all $i$.

nodes.name: Run $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ with $m^2$ colours; marginals unifor
nodes.statement: Consider the protocol $\mathcal{P}^\prime = \mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ on $C_n$ with $s^\prime = m^2$ colours and let $X^\prime \in_u \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:n/2}, we must have $H(X_i^\prime)=1$ and therefore $X_i^\prime$ is uniformly distributed over $\mathbb{Z}_{s^\prime}$ for all $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Run $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ with $m^2$ colours; marginals uniform by Theorem 3.4

nodes.name: Union bound on large colours
nodes.statement: By the union bound, $$ \mathbb{P}\left( X_i^\prime<s \; \forall \: i \right) \geq 1 - \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{P}(X_i^\prime \geq s) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{t}{m^2} = 1 - \frac{tn}{m^2}. $$

nodes.name: Restrict to $s$ colours via Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: Now, let $\mathcal{P}$ be a protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours such that $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P})$ for all colourings $c \in \mbox{Fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime)$ such that $c_i < s$ for all $i$ (such a protocol must exist by Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}).

nodes.name: Bound fix$(\mathcal{P})$
nodes.statement: For this protocol, \begin{align*} \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) & \geq \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime) \: \mathbb{P}\left( X_i^\prime<s \; \forall \: i \right) \\ & \geq \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}^\prime) \left( 1 - \frac{tn}{m^2} \right) \\ & = (s+t)^{n/2} \left( 1 - tn(s+t)^{-1} \right) \\ & \geq s^{n/2} \left( 1 - \frac{tn}{s} \right). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Even $n$: exact value
nodes.statement: For even $n$ we have $\mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = \frac{n}{2}$.

nodes.name: Odd $n$: apply Theorem 3.5 with $t=O(\sqrt s)$
nodes.statement: For odd $n$, let $m$ be the smallest positive integer such that $m^2 \geq s$. This gives $t = m^2-s = \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{s})$. If $\mathcal{P}$ is the protocol constructed in Theorem~\ref{thm:round_up}, then $$ \mbox{gn}(C_n,s) \geq \log_s\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \geq \frac{n}{2} + \log_s \left( 1 - \frac{tn}{s} \right) = \frac{n}{2} - \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{n}{\sqrt{s}\log_es} \right). $$

nodes.name: Reduce to small $\epsilon$; prove contrapositive
nodes.statement: For each $k$, it suffices to show this for all small enough $\epsilon$. Assume $7k\epsilon < 1$. We prove the contrapositive:

nodes.name: Case: some probability too large
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\mathbb{P}(Y=y) \geq \frac{1}{k} + \epsilon$ for at least one value $y$. Entropy is greatest when $Y$ is as uniformly distributed as possible. Therefore, \begin{align*} H(Y) & = - \sum_i \mathbb{P}(Y=i) \log_s \mathbb{P}(Y=i) \\ & \leq - \left( \tfrac{1}{k} + \epsilon \right) \log_s \left( \tfrac{1}{k}+\epsilon \right) - (k-1) \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \tfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} \right) \log_s \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \tfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} \right) \\ & = \log_s k - \left( \tfrac{1}{k} + \epsilon \right) \log_s( 1 + k\epsilon ) - \left( \tfrac{k-1}{k} - \epsilon \right) \log_s \left( 1 - \tfrac{k\epsilon}{k-1} \right). \intertext{Since $0 < k\epsilon < \frac{1}{7}$, we can use the identity, $-\log_s(1-\gamma) \leq (\gamma + \frac{5}{9}\gamma^2)\log_es$ (valid for $|\gamma| \leq 1/7$), to simplify this expression.} H(Y) & \leq \log_sk - \frac{k\epsilon^2}{9} \left( 4 - 5k\epsilon + \tfrac{4}{k-1} + \tfrac{5k\epsilon}{(k-1)^2} \right)\log_es \\ & \leq \log_sk - \frac{k\epsilon^2}{3}\log_es. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Case: some probability too small
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\mathbb{P}(Y=y) \leq \frac{1}{k} - \epsilon$ for at least one value $y$. The entropy would be greatest when $Y$ is as uniformly distributed as possible. Therefore, \begin{align*} H(Y) & = - \sum_i \mathbb{P}(Y=i) \log_s \mathbb{P}(Y=i) \\ & \leq - \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \epsilon \right) \log_s \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \epsilon \right) -(k-1) \left( \tfrac{1}{k} + \tfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} \right) \log_s \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \tfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} \right) \\ & = \log_sk - \left( \tfrac{1}{k} - \epsilon \right) \log_s ( 1 - k\epsilon ) - \left( \tfrac{k-1}{k} + \epsilon \right) \log_s \left( 1 + \tfrac{k\epsilon}{k-1} \right). \intertext{We can use the identity, $-\log_s(1-\gamma) \leq (\gamma + \frac{5}{9}\gamma^2)\log_es$, again to simplify this expression. } H(Y) & \leq \log_sk - \tfrac{k\epsilon^2}{9} \left( 4 - 5k\epsilon + \tfrac{4}{k-1} - \tfrac{5k\epsilon}{(k-1)^2} \right) \log_es\\ & \leq \log_sk - \frac{k\epsilon^2}{3}\log_es. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Choose $\delta$
nodes.statement: In either case, $H(Y) < \log_s k - \delta$ for any $\delta < \frac{k\epsilon^2}{3}\log_es$.

nodes.name: $\delta_1$ is well defined
nodes.statement: The value $\delta_1=\delta_1(s) = \tfrac{1}{2} \min \big\{ I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) \; \big| \; f \mbox{ is a flat but not semi-perfect} \big\}$ is well-defined for any $s \geq 2$, because there are only a finite number of functions $f : \mathbb{Z}_s^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_s$, and at least one of them is flat and not semi-perfect hence we can take the minimum of these. For example, the function $f(x,y) = x+y$ (mod $s$) is flat but not semi-perfect.

nodes.name: Choose $\epsilon$ small
nodes.statement: First, let $\epsilon < \frac{1}{s^2(s+2)}$, so that $$ \frac{1}{s^2} - (s-1)\epsilon > \frac{1}{s^2} - (s+1)\epsilon > \epsilon. $$

nodes.name: Claim: $f$ is flat
nodes.statement: We show that $f$ is flat by contradiction. Since $(Y_1,Y_3)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform: \begin{itemize} \item If $| f^{-1}(z) | \geq s+1$ then $$ \mathbb{P}(Y_2=z) = \mathbb{P}( (Y_1,Y_3) \in f^{-1}(z)) \geq (s+1) \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - \epsilon \right) = \tfrac{1}{s} + \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - (s+1)\epsilon \right) > \tfrac{1}{s} + \epsilon. $$ \item If $| f^{-1}(z) | \leq s-1$ then $$ \mathbb{P}(Y_2=z) = \mathbb{P}( (Y_1,Y_3) \in f^{-1}(z)) \leq (s-1) \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} + \epsilon \right) = \tfrac{1}{s} - \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - (s-1)\epsilon \right) < \tfrac{1}{s} - \epsilon. $$ \end{itemize} Both cases contradict the assumption that $Y_2$ is $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform. Therefore $f$ is a flat function and so $$I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) \geq 2\delta_1.$$

nodes.name: Large fibre gives too much mass
nodes.statement: If $| f^{-1}(z) | \geq s+1$ then $$ \mathbb{P}(Y_2=z) = \mathbb{P}( (Y_1,Y_3) \in f^{-1}(z)) \geq (s+1) \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - \epsilon \right) = \tfrac{1}{s} + \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - (s+1)\epsilon \right) > \tfrac{1}{s} + \epsilon. $$
nodes.statement_short: Large fibre gives too much mass

nodes.name: Small fibre gives too little mass
nodes.statement: If $| f^{-1}(z) | \leq s-1$ then $$ \mathbb{P}(Y_2=z) = \mathbb{P}( (Y_1,Y_3) \in f^{-1}(z)) \leq (s-1) \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} + \epsilon \right) = \tfrac{1}{s} - \left( \tfrac{1}{s^2} - (s-1)\epsilon \right) < \tfrac{1}{s} - \epsilon. $$
nodes.statement_short: Small fibre gives too little mass

nodes.name: So $f$ is flat
nodes.statement: Both cases contradict the assumption that $Y_2$ is $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform. Therefore $f$ is a flat function and so $$I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) \geq 2\delta_1.$$

nodes.name: Continuity of mutual information
nodes.statement: Moreover, since $(Y_1,Y_3)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $U$ and $(Y_1,Y_3)$ differ in distribution by less than $\epsilon$. Since mutual information is continuous, we can choose $\epsilon$ small enough so that $$ \big| I(U_1;U_2|f(U)) - I(Y_1;Y_3|Y_2) \big| \leq \delta_1. $$

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Then, by the triangle inequality, $I(Y_1;Y_3|Y_2) \geq \delta_1$.

nodes.name: Reduce using $h(i)\le1$
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:H(X),h(i)}, it suffices to show $H_1^5 \leq h(1)+h(3)+h(5)+h(2,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3)$.

nodes.name: List Shannon inequalities and determinism identities
nodes.statement: By Shannon's Inequality (Proposition~\ref{prop:known_entropy_results}) we have: \begin{align} h(2,3,4) + h(3) & = h(2,3) + h(3,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3), \\ h(1,2,3,4) + h(2,3) & \leq h(1,2,3) + h(2,3,4), \\ \mbox{and} \quad h(2,3,4,5) + h(3,4) & \leq h(2,3,4) + h(3,4,5). \\ \intertext{Also, since $X_i = f_i(X_{i-1},X_{i+1})$ for $i=2,3,4$ respectively we have:} h(1,2,3) &= h(1,3) \leq h(1) + h(3), \\ h(2,3,4) & = h(2,4), \\ \mbox{and} \quad h(3,4,5) &= h(3,5) \leq h(3) + h(5). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: List Shannon inequalities and determinism identities

nodes.name: Sum them
nodes.statement: The required result is the sum of equations (\ref{eq:mutual_information}), (\ref{eq:shannon12}), (\ref{eq:shannon23}), (\ref{eq:func1}), (\ref{eq:func2}) and (\ref{eq:func3}).

nodes.name: WLOG $j=1$; three cases
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality let $j=1$. There are $3$ cases.

nodes.name: Non-uniform marginal
nodes.statement: If, for any $i \in \{ 1,2,3,4,5 \}$, the variable $X_i$ is not $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $h(i) \leq 1 - \delta_2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:delta}). In this case, by Lemma~\ref{lem:H_j^k<sum(h(i))}, $$ H_1^5 \leq \sum_{i=1}^5 h(i) \leq 5 - \delta_2. $$

nodes.name: Non-uniform pair
nodes.statement: If $(X_2,X_4)$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, then $h(2,4) \leq 2-\delta_2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:delta}). Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{lem:shannon}, we have $$ H_1^5 \leq 3 + h(2,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3) \leq 5-\delta_2. $$

nodes.name: Non-semi-perfect $f_3$
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $X_2,X_3,X_4$ are each $(s,\epsilon)$-uniform and $(X_2,X_4)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform and $f_3$ is not semi-perfect. In this case, by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha}, we have $I(X_{j+1};X_{j+3}|X_{j+2}) \geq \delta_1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:shannon}, we have $$ H_1^5 \leq 3 + h(2,4) - I(X_2;X_4|X_3) \leq 5-\delta_1. $$

nodes.name: Combine with $\delta=\min$
nodes.statement: In all cases, we have $H_1^5 \leq 5 - \delta$ because $\delta = \min\{ \delta_1 , \delta_2 \}$.

nodes.name: WLOG $j=1$; cases
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality let $j=1$. We treat each case individually, and use Lemma~\ref{lem:one_non-semi-perfect_function}.

nodes.name: Defect at $f_3$
nodes.statement: If $f_3$ is not semi-perfect or $(X_2,X_4)$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform then \begin{align*} H_1^7 & = h(1,2,3,4,5,6) + h(2,3,4,5,6,7) \\ & = h(1,2,3,4,6) + h(2,3,4,5,7) \\ & \leq H_1^5 + h(6) + h(7) \\ & \leq (5 - \delta) + 1 + 1. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Defect at $f_4$
nodes.statement: If $f_4$ is not semi-perfect or $(X_3,X_5)$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform then \begin{align*} H_1^7 & = h(1,2,3,4,5,6) + h(2,3,4,5,6,7) \\ & = h(1,3,4,5,6) + h(2,3,4,5,7) \\ & \leq h(1) + H_2^6 + h(7) \\ & \leq 1 + (5 - \delta) + 1. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Defect at $f_5$
nodes.statement: If $f_5$ is not semi-perfect or $(X_4,X_6)$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform then \begin{align*} H_1^7 & = h(1,2,3,4,5,6) + h(2,3,4,5,6,7) \\ & = h(1,3,4,5,6) + h(2,4,5,6,7) \\ & \leq h(1) + h(2) + H_3^7 \\ & \leq 1 + 1 + (5 - \delta). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Window decomposition with Lemmas 2.9 and 4.8
nodes.statement: Let $m$ be an odd integer such that $m > \delta^{-1}$ and $7m \leq n$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:H(X)=sum(H)} and Lemma~\ref{lem:at_least_one_non-semi-perfect_function}, we have \begin{align*} 2H(X) & \leq \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} H_{7j+1}^{7j+7} + \sum_{i=7m}^{n-1} h(i) \\ & \leq m(7 - \delta) + (n-7m) \\ & = n - m \delta. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Entropy below $(n-1)/2$
nodes.statement: Since $m > \delta^{-1}$, this means that $H(X) < \frac{n-1}{2}$.

nodes.name: Convert to fixed number
nodes.statement: Therefore $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) < s^{(n-1)/2}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:H(X),h(i)}.

nodes.name: Conditional independence from semi-perfectness
nodes.statement: Let $U = (U_1,U_2) \in_u \mathbb{Z}_s^2$ and for a given $z$, let $L = L(f,z)$ and $R = R(f,z)$. Since $f$ is semi-perfect, we have $I(U_1,U_2 \; | \; f(U))=0$. Therefore, $U_1$ and $U_2$ are conditionally independent given $f(U)$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Fibre is $L\times R$
nodes.statement: For any $x \in L$ and any $y \in R$, we must have \begin{align*}& \mathbb{P}(U_1=x \wedge U_2=y | f(U)=z) = \mathbb{P}(U_1=x | f(U)=z)\mathbb{P}(U_2=y | f(U)=z) > 0, \\ &\mbox{and }f^{-1}(z) = L \times R.\end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Compute $\mathbb{P}(f(U)=z)$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $U_1$ and $U_2$ are independently uniformly distributed over $\mathbb{Z}_s$ and $U$ is uniformly distributed over $\mathbb{Z}_s^2$, we have $$ \frac{1}{s} = \mathbb{P}( f(U)=z) = \mathbb{P}( U_1 \in L \wedge U_2 \in R) = \mathbb{P}( U_1 \in L) \times \mathbb{P}(U_2 \in R) = \frac{|L|}{s} \times \frac{|R|}{s}. $$
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: $|L||R|=s$
nodes.statement: Therefore, $|L||R| = s$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Assume unequal fibre sizes; define $S_0,S_3$
nodes.statement: We proceed by contradiction. Let $S_0 = \{ c_0 | f_1(c_0,c_2)=c_1 \}$ and $S_3 = \{ c_3 | f_2(c_1,c_3)=c_2 \}$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: WLOG $|S_0|<|S_3|$
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality assume $|S_0|<|S_3|$ so since $|S_0| < s$ we must have $|S_3| > \left( 1 + \frac{1}{s} \right)|S_0|$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Upper bound via $(X_0,X_2)$
nodes.statement: Now since $(X_0,X_2)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, $$ \mathbb{P}( X_1=c_1 \wedge X_2=c_2) = \sum_{x \in S_0} \mathbb{P}\big( (X_0,X_2) = (x,c_2) \big) \leq |S_0| \left( \frac{1}{s^2} + \epsilon \right). $$
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Lower bound via $(X_1,X_3)$
nodes.statement: Similarly, since $(X_1,X_3)$ is $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform, $$ \mathbb{P}( X_1=c_1 \wedge X_2=c_2) = \sum_{x \in S_3}\mathbb{P}\big( (X_1,X_3) = (c_1,x) \big) \geq |S_3| \left( \frac{1}{s^2} - \epsilon \right). $$
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: However, since $\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}$, this implies $$ 1 + \frac{1}{s} < \frac{|S_3|}{|S_0|} \leq \frac{s^{-2}+\epsilon}{s^{-2}-\epsilon} \leq \frac{\frac{1}{s^2}+\frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}}{\frac{1}{s^2}-\frac{1}{s^2(2s+1)}} = 1 + \frac{1}{s}, $$ which is a contradiction.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: WLOG $j=0$; fix $c_0,c_0'$
nodes.statement: We proceed by contradiction. Without loss of generality, assume $j=0$ and fix $c_0,c_0^\prime \in \mathbb{Z}_s$ arbitrarily.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Choose preimages and $c_0''$
nodes.statement: Now choose $c_{-1},c_1\in \mathbb{Z}_s$ such that $f_0(c_{-1},c_1)=c_0$ and choose $c_{-1}^\prime,c_1^\prime \in \mathbb{Z}_s$ such that $f_0(c_{-1}^\prime ,c_1^\prime)=c_0^\prime$. Also let $c_0^{\prime\prime} = f_0(c_{-1}^\prime ,c_1)$.

nodes.name: Equate $L$- and $R$-sizes via Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: Now by Lemma~\ref{lem:two_semi-perfect_functions}, \begin{align*} |L(f_0,c_0)| = | \{ x | f_0(x,c_1)=c_0 \} | = | \{ x | f_1(c_0,x)=c_1 \} | & = |R(f_1,c_1)| \\ \mbox{and} \qquad |L(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})| = | \{ x | f_0(x,c_1)=c_0^{\prime\prime} \} | = | \{ x | f_1(c_0^{\prime\prime},x)=c_1 \} | & = |R(f_1,c_1)|. \end{align*} Similarly \begin{align*} |R(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})| = | \{ x | f_0(c_{-1}^{\prime},x)=c_0^{\prime\prime} \} | = | \{ x | f_{-1}(x,c_0^{\prime\prime})=c_{-1}^{\prime} \} | & = |L(f_{-1},c_{-1}^{\prime})| \\ \mbox{and} \qquad |R(f_0,c_0^{\prime})| = | \{ x | f_0(c_{-1}^{\prime},x)=c_0^{\prime} \} | = | \{ x | f_{-1}(x,c_0^{\prime})=c_{-1}^{\prime} \} | & = |L(f_{-1},c_{-1}^{\prime})|. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Use $|L||R|=s$ to equate all $L$- and $R$-sizes, so $f_0$ is
nodes.statement: Recall that $|L(f_0,z)|\cdot |R(f_0,z)|=s$ for all $z\in \mathbb{Z}_s$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:LR=s}). Therefore, $|R(f_0,c_0^{\prime})|=|R(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})|$ if and only if $|L(f_0,c_0^{\prime})|=|L(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})|$. Hence, $$ |L(f_0,c_0)| = |L(f_0,c_0^{\prime\prime})| = |L(f_0,c_0^{\prime})|. $$ Similarly, $|R(f_0,c_0)| = |R(f_0,c_0^\prime)|$ (for arbitrary $c_0,c_0^\prime \in \mathbb{Z}_s$) and therefore $f_0$ is a perfect function.

nodes.name: WLOG $j=2$, $l\le r$, so $l\le a$
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, assume $j=2$. Since $f_2$ is perfect, let $l = |L(f_2,z)|$ and $r=|R(f_2,z)|$. Without loss of generality, assume $l \leq r$ and therefore $l \leq a$.
