nodes.name: Bound $h(1,2)\le\log_s(ls)$
nodes.statement: Then $X_2$ takes at most $s$ different values and $X_1$, conditioned on $X_2=z$ for any $z \in \mathbb{Z}_s$, takes at most $l$ different values. Therefore, the pair $(X_1,X_2)$ takes at most $ls$ different values in $\mathbb{Z}_s^2$ and $h(1,2) \leq \log_s(ls)$.
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Bound $H(X)$
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} H(X) & = h(1,2,3, \ldots ,n) \\ & = h(1,2,4,6, \ldots ,n-3,n-1) \\ & \leq h(1,2) + \sum_{i=1}^{(n-3)/2} h(2i+2) \\ & \leq \log_s(ls) + \frac{n-3}{2}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Conclude fix bound
nodes.statement: Therefore $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) = s^{H(X)} \leq ls^{(n-1)/2} \leq as^{(n-1)/2}$.

nodes.name: Set $N$; two cases
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ be the values given in Definition~\ref{defn:epsilon,delta}, let $N = 7(\delta^{-1}+2)$ and let $\mathcal{P} = (f_1,f_2, \ldots ,f_n)$ be any non-trivial protocol on $C_n$ with $s$ colours. We have two cases:
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Case one: defects everywhere
nodes.statement: [Case one] For all $j$, either: \begin{itemize} \item at least one of the functions $f_{j-1}$, $f_j$ and $f_{j+1}$ is not semi-perfect or \item at least one of $(X_{j-2},X_j)$, $(X_{j-1},X_{j+1})$, $(X_j,X_{j+2})$ is not $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 5 Guessing numbers of large odd cycles

nodes.name: Case two: a good window exists
nodes.statement: [Case two] There exists some $j$ such that: \begin{itemize} \item the functions $f_{j-1}$, $f_j$ and $f_{j+1}$ are all semi-perfect and \item $(X_{j-2},X_j)$, $(X_{j-1},X_{j+1})$ and $(X_j,X_{j+2})$ are all $(s^2,\epsilon)$-uniform. \end{itemize}

nodes.statement_short: Case two: a good window exists

nodes.name: Case one via Lemma 4.9
nodes.statement: For case one, we can conclude that $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \leq s^{(n-1)/2} \leq \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:many_non-semi-perfect_functions}.

nodes.name: Case two via Lemmas 5.4, 5.5
nodes.statement: In case two, $f_j$ must be a perfect function (Lemma~\ref{lem:three_semi-perfect_functions}) and then $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}) \leq as^{(n-1)/2} = \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:one_perfect_function}).

nodes.name: $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ optimal
nodes.statement: In either case, $\mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P}_{fcp}) \geq \mbox{fix}(\mathcal{P})$. Hence $\mathcal{P}_{fcp}$ is optimal.

nodes.name: Lower bound from Theorem 5.6
nodes.statement: Write $a=s/b$. First by Theorem~\ref{thm:n_large}, $\mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = (n-1)/2 +\log_sa$ for all large enough odd $n$. Therefore, $$ \beta(C_n,s) \geq n - \mbox{gn}(C_n,s) = \frac{n-1}{2} + \log_sb. $$
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information

nodes.name: Set up explicit code
nodes.statement: To show that we in fact get equality, we define a set of $bs^{(n-1)/2}$ possible messages with which the sender can solve the index coding with side information problem on $C_n$. Let $\phi$ and $\psi$ be defined as in Definition~\ref{defn:phi_and_psi}. This means that $\phi \times \psi$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{Z}_a \times \mathbb{Z}_b$ to $\mathbb{Z}_s$. Now for any colouring $c = (c_1,c_2, \ldots ,c_n) \in \mathbb{Z}_s^n$ let the sender broadcast the following values:
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information

nodes.name: Broadcast pair sums
nodes.statement: For $i=1,2,3, \ldots ,\tfrac{n-1}{2}$, the sender broadcasts the residue $\phi(c_{2i-1})+\phi(c_{2i})$ modulo $a$ and the residue $\psi(c_{2i})+\psi(c_{2i+1})$ modulo $b$.
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information

nodes.name: Broadcast link residue
nodes.statement: Additionally, the sender broadcasts the residue $\psi(c_1)+\phi(c_n)$ modulo $b$.
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information

nodes.name: Count messages
nodes.statement: The sender broadcasts $\frac{n-1}{2}$ residues modulo $a$ and $\frac{n+1}{2}$ residues modulo $b$, and so the total number of possible messages that the sender might send is $$ m = a^{(n-1)/2}b^{(n+1)/2} = bs^{(n-1)/2}. $$
nodes.section: 6 An application to index coding with side information

nodes.name: Receivers decode
nodes.statement: Furthermore, each receiver, $v_i$, knows $c_{i-1}$ and $c_{i+1}$, and so can recover both $c_i$ because she can recover both $\phi(c_i)$ and $\psi(c_i)$.
